data.title: NICE backs PADCEV and KEYTRUDA combination
data.description:
Astellas Pharma has welcomed final draft guidance from NICE recommending pembrolizumab (KEYTRUDA) in combination with enfortumab vedotin (PADCEV) as a treatment option for adults with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) in England and Wales.

The recommendation covers use of the combination as neoadjuvant treatment before surgery, followed by continued treatment after radical cystectomy as adjuvant therapy, within its marketing authorisation.

According to Astellas, the decision provides a treatment option for eligible adults with MIBC regardless of whether they are able to receive cisplatin-based chemotherapy, which has traditionally been a standard treatment before surgery.

NICE concluded that there is sufficient evidence to demonstrate clinical benefit and cost effectiveness for the combination, supporting its routine use across the NHS in this patient population.

Bladder cancer is responsible for around 5,900 deaths annually in the UK and accounts for approximately 3% of all cancer deaths. Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is an aggressive form of the disease in which tumour cells spread beyond the bladder lining and into the surrounding muscle.

The condition is associated with a substantial risk of recurrence and disease progression despite treatment being given with curative intent. NICE has previously identified a need for treatments that can slow disease progression and prolong survival, particularly among patients who cannot receive cisplatin.

Dr Tim Patel, Medical Director at Astellas UK, said: “We welcome NICE’s recommendation for adults with muscle-invasive bladder cancer.”

He added: “This is an important step in expanding treatment options around surgery, including for people who are unable to receive cisplatin-based chemotherapy.”

Patel continued: “We remain committed to working with the NHS and the bladder cancer community to support timely access to treatment advances for patients who may benefit.”

PADCEV is an antibody-drug conjugate directed against Nectin-4, a protein highly expressed in bladder cancer cells. The therapy is already approved in several territories for urothelial cancer indications, including in combination with pembrolizumab.

In the EU, the combination of enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab is approved for adult patients with resectable muscle-invasive bladder cancer regardless of cisplatin eligibility.

data.title: First patient dosed in rectal cancer BT-001 trial
data.description:
Transgene and Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital, University of Copenhagen, have announced that the first patient has been dosed in a phase 1 clinical trial evaluating BT-001 in patients with proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) rectal cancer.

The investigator-sponsored OV-PRIME-R trial is assessing BT-001, an armed oncolytic virus administered through intratumoral injection, followed by intravenous pembrolizumab treatment. The study is focused on patients with localised pMMR rectal cancer, a population representing around 95% of rectal cancer cases and one that has historically shown limited response to immunotherapy alone.

The trial is designed to investigate the safety, tolerability and efficacy of neoadjuvant treatment with BT-001 combined with an anti-PD1 antibody before standard surgery.

Researchers hope that the approach could help address limitations associated with current treatment options. While neoadjuvant chemo-radiotherapy can reduce recurrence and preserve organs in some patients, fewer than 30% of patients achieve a complete response and some still experience distant recurrence.

BT-001 is being co-developed by Transgene and BioInvent. The therapy was created using Transgene’s Invir.IO platform and is engineered to express GM-CSF and BioInvent’s full-length anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody.

Henry G. Smith, Associate Professor and consultant surgeon at Abdominal Center K, Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital University of Copenhagen and Principal Investigator, said: “We are excited to launch this investigator-sponsored trial, which explores an innovative approach to treating rectal cancer in patients with proficient mismatch repair status.”

He added: “By combining BT-001, an armed oncolytic virus, with anti-PD-1 therapy, in patients with localized disease, we aim to enhance the immune response and potentially improve outcomes for patients by reducing the risks of relapse or even reducing the number who need surgery at all.”

Smith continued: “This study represents an important step toward more effective and less toxic treatment strategies for this underserved population.”

Emmanuelle Dochy, Chief Medical Officer of Transgene, explained: “We are proud to support this investigator-sponsored trial in collaboration with the University of Copenhagen, evaluating BT-001 in patients with rectal cancer at high risk of relapse and severe toxicities from standard of care.”

She added: “BT-001 has already demonstrated excellent tolerability and the ability to transform ‘cold’ tumors into biologically active ones. This study aims to further validate its potential to improve outcomes and quality of life for cancer patients.”

data.title: Cancer Grand Challenges launches AI research project
data.description:
Cancer scientists will begin testing an artificial intelligence ‘co-scientist’ designed to help generate new research ideas and accelerate discovery through an £8 million project funded by Cancer Research UK.

The initiative, known as Project AURORA, will see three international Cancer Grand Challenges teams assess whether AI can help tackle some of the most difficult questions in cancer research.

The teams will use the technology to investigate why some normal cells become cancerous, how the immune system can be better equipped to recognise and destroy tumours and how immune-cell therapies could be improved for childhood cancers.

Project AURORA uses agentic AI to search scientific literature and analyse research data. The system is designed to identify patterns, generate new scientific hypotheses and propose experiments to test those ideas.

Researchers will evaluate the AI-generated suggestions and conduct the most promising experiments in the laboratory. Findings from those studies will then be fed back into the system to help guide future research directions.

According to Cancer Research UK, the technology could also help scientists identify less promising avenues earlier, enabling resources to be focused on the most productive lines of investigation.

The project is funded through Cancer Grand Challenges, a global research initiative established by Cancer Research UK and the US National Cancer Institute. Development of the AI platform is being led by a team headed by Associate Professor Marinka Zitnik at Harvard Medical School.

Unlike conventional AI tools that respond to individual queries, the system is intended to plan and execute a sequence of research-related tasks while operating under human oversight.

Michelle Mitchell, Chief Executive of Cancer Research UK, said: “Behind every advance in our understanding of cancer are researchers asking difficult questions, testing ideas and following the evidence.”

She added: “AI offers new possibilities, but it takes skilled scientists to turn a promising idea into a discovery that can make a difference to people’s lives.”

Mitchell continued: “Through Cancer Grand Challenges, we’re bringing AI together with the expertise of outstanding researchers to tackle some of cancer’s toughest problems.”

She concluded: “Our ambition is to accelerate discoveries that could lead to new ways to prevent, diagnose and treat cancer.”

data.title: GENFIT highlights nangibotide potential in ACLF
data.description:
GENFIT has presented new clinical and scientific data supporting the development of nangibotide in acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), with a phase 2a proof-of-concept study expected to begin before the end of 2026 and top-line data anticipated in the second half of 2027.

The biopharmaceutical company unveiled the findings during a scientific meeting of leading ACLF experts held alongside AASLD The Liver Meeting in Denver.

Nangibotide is GENFIT’s lead investigational asset for ACLF, a severe condition characterised by systemic inflammation and multi-organ dysfunction. The therapy is designed to modulate triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1 (TREM-1), an amplifier of inflammation, with the aim of reducing excessive inflammatory responses without directly affecting immune recognition.

According to the company, activation of the TREM-1 pathway has been linked to progression from acute decompensation to ACLF and is associated with disease severity and poor outcomes.

GENFIT highlighted safety and efficacy findings generated across previous phase 2 studies of nangibotide in septic shock and COVID-19, involving a total of 416 exposed subjects.

The company reported an overall safety profile comparable to placebo and no identified safety signals. In a subgroup of 118 septic shock patients with elevated soluble TREM-1 levels, nangibotide was associated with a greater reduction in Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score compared with placebo, alongside favourable trends in mortality and other clinical outcomes.

In a separate study involving 219 patients with COVID-19, treatment with nangibotide was associated with improved clinical status and lower day 28 mortality.

Professor Jennifer C. Lai, Endowed Professor of Liver Health & Transplantation at the University of California, San Francisco, said: “The unmet need in ACLF remains tremendous, particularly for patients in the ICU who can rapidly progress to multi-organ failure.”

She added: “What is especially exciting about nangibotide is that we are not starting from scratch: the program already benefits from substantial phase 2 clinical experience and proof-of-concept in acute inflammatory conditions characterized by organ dysfunction.”

Lai continued: “This gives us a rare opportunity to bring an already extensively studied clinical-stage candidate into ACLF and explore whether those signals can translate into meaningful benefit for these critically ill patients.”

data.title: Nxera signs $1.47bn AbbVie licensing deal
data.description:
Nxera Pharma has entered into an exclusive global licensing agreement with AbbVie for NXE0033744, an investigational oral EP4 receptor agonist being developed for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie will receive exclusive worldwide rights to develop and commercialise the candidate for IBD. Nxera will receive an upfront payment of $100 million and could earn up to a further $1.37 billion in development and commercial milestone payments, in addition to tiered royalties on net sales.

The transaction remains subject to customary antitrust clearances, including requirements under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act.

NXE0033744 was discovered using Nxera’s proprietary NxWave drug discovery platform and is designed to selectively activate EP4 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract.

The therapy is being developed to address unmet needs among patients with IBD who do not achieve adequate disease control with existing treatments.

According to Nxera, the candidate aims to induce anti-inflammatory effects while promoting epithelial barrier homeostasis and mucosal healing. The company believes this could provide a differentiated mechanism of action compared with currently available therapies.

A phase 1 study has already been completed, generating data that supported a gut-selective profile and target engagement.

Christopher Cargill, President and CEO of Nxera Pharma, said: “This agreement with AbbVie marks a milestone in the continued development of NXE0033744 and reflects the potential of our NxWave platform to generate differentiated medicines for significant unmet needs.”

He added: “NXE0033744 is built on a novel biological approach, designed to activate EP4 locally in the gut to support epithelial barrier homeostasis and mucosal healing, potentially offering a differentiated mechanism of action from existing treatments.”

Cargill continued: “AbbVie is already an important partner to Nxera through our ongoing neuroscience discovery collaboration, and this agreement is a strong vote of confidence in NxWave’s ability to consistently deliver.”

He explained: “With its deep expertise and proven track record in immunological diseases, and global clinical development, we believe AbbVie is the ideal partner to advance the program globally and determine whether this biology can translate into measurable, life-changing outcomes for people with IBD.”

Cargill concluded: “The upfront payment, together with potential near-term milestone payments, will further strengthen our financial position while enabling Nxera to share in the future success of NXE0033744 and the value it may create.”

data.title: Santersus advances nucleoCapture into pivotal sepsis study
data.description:
Santersus is advancing NUC‑CAP, a multicentre, randomised pivotal study of NucleoCapture, its investigational extracorporeal blood‑purification technology, in critically ill patients with sepsis and respiratory failure.

The trial is expected to enrol up to 350 patients across clinical sites in the United States and Europe, with Axcellant appointed as global CRO to support international execution.

Participants will be randomized 1:1 to receive either standard of care alone or standard of care plus NucleoCapture. The study will assess device‑related safety and a primary effectiveness endpoint combining all‑cause mortality through day 28 with organ support‑free days through day 28, analysed using win‑ratio methodology.

The aim is to determine whether selectively removing circulating neutrophil extracellular traps can improve outcomes for patients requiring intensive care.

NucleoCapture is designed to remove NETs from the bloodstream through selective extracorporeal adsorption. NETs contribute to innate immune defence but have also been associated with inflammatory and thrombotic processes and organ injury when excessive or dysregulated.

The clinical significance of targeting NETs remains to be established. According to World Health Organization estimates for 2017, ~48.9 million people developed sepsis worldwide and 11 million deaths were associated with the condition.

The pivotal programme follows earlier development, including completion of a first‑in‑human exploratory study. In 2022, NucleoCapture received FDA Breakthrough Device Designation as an adjunctive treatment to antibiotics in sepsis.

James Ladtkow, Chief Executive Officer of Santersus, said: “The advancement of NUC-CAP into pivotal development is a significant milestone for Santersus because it moves NucleoCapture into a rigorous, multinational clinical program designed to evaluate endpoints that matter in the treatment of critically ill patients.”

He added: “Our objective is to build a robust body of clinical evidence around a differentiated therapeutic approach: directly removing circulating NETs that are associated with inflammatory, thrombotic and organ-damaging processes.”

Wojciech Kula, CEO of Axcellant, said: “We are pleased to support Santersus in the global execution of NUC-CAP.”

He continued: “The study represents an important clinical undertaking in a critically ill patient population, and our team will bring integrated clinical-development capabilities to support disciplined execution across participating regions.”

Santersus is targeting an interim analysis in Q4 2027, followed by potential CE certification and an EU launch in Q2 2028. PMA submission is planned for Q2 2029, with potential FDA approval and a US launch in Q4 2029.

data.title: Myeloma fund launches with £15m initial backing
data.description:
A new £30 million venture philanthropy fund is being launched to accelerate the development of treatments, diagnostics and technologies aimed at finding a cure for myeloma, an incurable blood cancer that claims eight lives every day in the UK.

The Jacquelin Forbes-Nixon Myeloma Fund is being established by the DFN Foundation with £15 million already committed. The funding includes £10 million from the foundation and a further £5 million from philanthropist and investor David Forbes-Nixon OBE, subject to matched support from other donors.

The fund will seek an additional £15 million from philanthropic partners and will focus on supporting early-stage science and biotechnology ventures that may be considered too early or high-risk for traditional commercial investment.

Unlike conventional charitable donations, the fund will invest philanthropic capital in promising ventures and reinvest any financial returns into future projects through an evergreen model designed to support ongoing myeloma innovation.

The initiative forms part of the wider Jacquelin Forbes-Nixon Myeloma Mission, which aims to deliver a functional cure for an increasing proportion of patients over the next decade and beyond.

Myeloma develops in the bone marrow and affects around 16 people every day in the UK. The disease remains difficult to diagnose, with around a third of patients only diagnosed following an emergency presentation.

David Forbes-Nixon OBE, founder and Chairman of the DFN Foundation and the JFN Myeloma Fund, said: “When my mother Jacquelin died from myeloma, I promised her I would do everything I could to help find a cure.”

He added: “Twenty years later, science has advanced enormously, but too many promising ideas still struggle to secure investment because they are considered too early or too risky.”

Forbes-Nixon continued: “That is why the DFN Foundation is committing £10 million, and I am personally committing a further £5 million.”

He explained: “We now want others to match that commitment and help us build a £30 million fund.”

Dr Stephanie Oestreich, Managing Director of the JFN Myeloma Fund, said: “There is outstanding science emerging in myeloma, but excellent science does not automatically become a treatment.”

She added: “Success in this area will ultimately be measured by whether we can get better treatments to patients faster. That’s the space this fund will be operating in.”

data.title: Octane and Currus automate CUR‑001 manufacturing on cocoon platform
data.description:
Octane Biotech and Currus Biologics have automated the manufacturing process for CUR‑001 on Octane’s Cocoon platform, establishing a closed, reliable process to support consistent production as the therapy enters clinical development.

The milestone follows FDA clearance of Currus’ IND application, enabling a first‑in‑human, open‑label phase 1 basket trial in mesothelin‑positive advanced refractory solid tumours, with first patient dosing expected in early 2027.

CUR‑001 is the first clinical programme from Currus’ BEAT platform, combining an autologous, FLAG‑tagged CAR T‑cell therapy targeting mesothelin with a BEAT bispecific antibody. The design engages CAR T‑cells and antigen‑presenting cells to activate T‑cells in lymphoid tissue and counter the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment that has limited CAR T‑cell therapy in solid tumours.

The companies have transferred the manufacturing process onto the Cocoon, Octane’s automated system for patient‑specific cell therapies. Moving to the platform significantly reduced hands‑on operator time and viral vector requirements, two major cost drivers in autologous CAR T‑cell manufacturing.

Sam Cobb, Chief Executive Officer of Currus Biologics, said: “Getting IND clearance was a significant step forward. Ensuring we can make CUR-001 reliably, patient after patient, is now our focus.”

He added: “The success of an autologous therapy depends heavily on the process behind it. Moving CUR-001 onto the Cocoon gives us a consistent, closed process as we head into the clinic, and a manufacturing model that can grow with the programme.”

Louis Briggs, Vice President, Octane Biotech, explained: “Currus has a smart answer to one of the hardest problems in cell therapy, which is getting CAR T-cells to work in solid tumours.”

He continued: “Automating CUR-001 on the Cocoon means fewer manual steps, less variability between batches and a process built to scale from phase 1 onward. We’re proud to support Currus as CUR-001 moves toward its first patients.”

CUR‑001 will be manufactured for the phase 1 trial at Cell Therapies Pty Ltd in Melbourne, where technology transfer has been completed and operational readiness established.

data.title: Teva expands biosimilars alliance with Samsung Bioepis
data.description:
Teva Pharmaceutical Industries and Samsung Bioepis have announced a new licensing and commercialisation agreement covering two FDA-approved immunology biosimilars in the US, further expanding their existing partnership in the biosimilars market.

Under the agreement, Teva will gain US commercialisation rights to ETICOVO (etanercept-ykro) when the deal closes and will assume commercialisation rights to infliximab-abda in the third quarter of 2027.

Samsung Bioepis will retain responsibility for regulatory oversight and manufacturing of both products. The transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory approvals, and is expected to close by the end of 2026.

The two treatments are biosimilars referencing Enbrel and Remicade respectively and are intended for the treatment of a range of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

Richard Francis, President and CEO of Teva, said: “This agreement strengthens our collaboration with Samsung Bioepis and will expand our U.S. immunology portfolio with two additional biologic treatment options.”

He added: “Biosimilars are an important part of our Pivot to Growth strategy, helping us build a stronger portfolio while expanding access to high-quality medicines.”

Francis continued: “Together, we have an opportunity to bring more treatment choices to patients living with chronic inflammatory conditions.”

Kyung-Ah Kim, President and Chief Executive Officer of Samsung Bioepis, explained: “We are delighted to expand our strategic alliance with Teva to strengthen the commercial footprint of our immunology portfolio in the U.S.”

Kim added: “Infliximab-abda has established a proven track record of clinical efficacy and supply reliability since its launch, while ETICOVO represents an FDA-approved therapy poised to broaden treatment choices for patients.”

She continued: “By pairing our dedication to high-quality biologic development and manufacturing with Teva’s commercial reach across U.S. healthcare channels, we aim to ensure uninterrupted treatment continuity for existing patients and bring sustainable value to the US healthcare system.”

The latest agreement builds on several biosimilar partnerships between the companies. In 2025, they agreed a US commercialisation deal for EPYSQLI, while during 2026 they announced agreements covering OPUVIZ in Canada and up to six biosimilar candidates currently in early-stage development.

data.title: Panthera expands Glasgow clinical research capacity
data.description:
Panthera has opened its expanded Glasgow Clinical Research Centre at the Health Innovation Hub, increasing capacity for commercial clinical research across Glasgow and the west of Scotland.

The UK’s largest independent clinical trial SMO marked the opening on 22 October with guests from healthcare, academia, government and industry. Dr Zubir Ahmed MP attended as Guest of Honour.

The purpose‑built centre includes eight clinical rooms, laboratory facilities and modern office space to support delivery of phase II and III trials for pharmaceutical sponsors and CROs. Panthera relocated from the Clinical Innovation Zone at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital earlier this year, with the new site expected to broaden opportunities for eligible patients to participate in studies of investigational treatments.

During the opening, Dr Ahmed spoke about the importance of clinical research infrastructure in maintaining Scotland’s leadership in medical research. Guests toured the facility and met Panthera staff to discuss trial delivery and ways to expand patient participation.

Dr Zubir Ahmed MP, Member of Parliament for Glasgow South West, said: “It was a pleasure to join Panthera to celebrate the opening of its expanded clinical research centre in Glasgow South West. I have first-hand experience of Glasgow’s proud history of medical innovation. Investment in facilities like this helps ensure our city remains at the forefront of developing new treatments and improving healthcare”

He added: “Clinical research has the potential to make a real difference to people’s lives, and it is particularly encouraging to see opportunities for patients in our local communities to participate in trials that could help shape the future of medicine.”

Stuart Young, CEO of Panthera, commented: “We are delighted to celebrate the official opening of our expanded Glasgow centre alongside colleagues and partners from across Scotland’s healthcare and life sciences community.”

He continued: “Glasgow has an outstanding reputation for medical research and innovation. This investment increases our capacity to deliver commercial clinical trials and reflects our confidence in the city’s research expertise.”

The centre sits within the Health Innovation Hub, developed by Kadans Science Partner with the Living Laboratory for Precision Medicine, supporting collaboration across Glasgow’s life sciences sector.
